outline: Social Sciences — Communication and interpersonal skills, including health literacy
Patient-centered communication skills — enabling patient behaviors, education and counseling
mechanism: Teach-back is a health-literacy communication method in which the clinician asks the patient to explain in their own words what they need to know or do. For device-based instructions, the related show-me method asks the patient to demonstrate the task. The purpose is to verify that the clinician explained the information clearly and to identify misunderstandings that require re-explanation; simply asking whether the patient understands or has questions does not reliably assess comprehension.
vignette: A 45-year-old man with asthma is prescribed a new metered-dose inhaler. The physician explains when the inhaler should be used and demonstrates the technique. Before ending the visit, the physician wants to determine whether the instructions were communicated clearly and whether the patient can correctly use the device at home.
lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next statement by the physician?
correct: “I want to make sure I explained this clearly. Please show me how you will use the inhaler when you are at home.”
distractors: “Do you understand how to use the inhaler?”
“Do you have any questions about what I just explained?”
“Please repeat my instructions back to me word for word.”
“Read the package instructions again at home and call the office if something is unclear.”
distractor_notes: A yes/no question such as asking whether the patient understands does not reliably reveal misunderstanding. Teach-back asks the patient to explain or demonstrate what they will do.
Inviting questions is useful but does not directly verify comprehension; patients may report that they have no questions despite incomplete understanding.
Teach-back is not rote repetition or a memory test. AHRQ emphasizes that the patient should explain in their own words or demonstrate the task rather than merely parrot the clinician's wording.

Written instructions can supplement education but do not replace confirmation of understanding before the patient leaves. For a new device, directly observing the patient demonstrate use is a stronger check of communication.
key_expl: The physician should use teach-back/show-me. AHRQ defines teach-back as asking patients to explain in their own words what they need to know or do, and specifically gives inhaler use as an example in which the patient can be asked to show how the device will be used at home. This approach checks whether the clinician's explanation was clear and allows immediate correction of misunderstandings. MedlinePlus likewise advises patients to have a clinician or pharmacist demonstrate inhaler use and to have their technique checked.
objective: Use teach-back/show-me to verify patient understanding of inhaler instructions: ask the patient to explain or demonstrate how the device will be used rather than relying on yes/no comprehension questions, passive handouts, or verbatim repetition.
clues: physician has already explained and demonstrated use
goal is to confirm understanding before the visit ends
device technique can be directly demonstrated
